lessons.title: What is Playwright?
lessons.story: Imagine a tiny robot friend who can open a web browser and use it exactly like you do: type, click, scroll. You write a to-do list, and the robot follows it and tells you if something looks wrong. That robot is `Playwright`. It was made by Microsoft and works with Chrome, Firefox and Safari (WebKit).
lessons.codeCaption: Same story, new words: launch a browser, open a tab (`page`), visit a site, close.
points: No `chromedriver.exe` to download or match with your browser version. Playwright brings its own browsers.
It runs on Node.js. You write in TypeScript, which is JavaScript with types (like Java!).
One API for Chromium, Firefox and WebKit.

quiz.question: Which one do you NOT need to manage yourself in Playwright?
quiz.why: Playwright downloads and manages its own browsers, so no driver juggling.

deep.text: How does it actually work?

Selenium talks to a separate driver program (chromedriver) over HTTP, and the driver talks to the browser. Playwright skips the middle-man: it keeps one fast connection open to the browser and sends commands over it. That's why it is quicker and why it can notice things like network calls and page loads.
The 4 building blocks

`Browser` is the whole browser program. A `BrowserContext` is a clean profile inside it (like an incognito window: its own cookies and storage). A `Page` is one tab inside a context. A `Locator` is a pointer to something on a page.

deep.title: Browser → Context → Page
deep.code:
const browser = await chromium.launch();          // the browser program
const context = await browser.newContext();       // a clean profile
const page = await context.newPage();             // a tab
const other = await browser.newContext();         // totally separate user

deep.text: When you use `@playwright/test`, it creates the browser, context and page for you for every test. You only do it by hand in scripts.
Playwright is not Selenium-compatible. Your Java `WebDriver` code can't be reused, but the ideas (locators, waits, page objects) all carry over.

lessons.title: Why people love it over Selenium
lessons.story: In Selenium, you stand at a door and keep asking, "Is it open yet? Is it open yet?" (that's `WebDriverWait`). In Playwright, the robot is patient. It waits by itself until the door opens, then walks in. Less asking, fewer tests that fail for silly reasons.
lessons.javaCode:
WebDriverWait wait = new WebDriverWait(driver, Duration.ofSeconds(10));
wait.until(ExpectedConditions.elementToBeClickable(By.id("login"))).click();
lessons.code:
// Playwright waits for the button automatically
await page.locator('#login').click();
lessons.codeCaption: Two lines of waiting code in Selenium became zero.
points: Auto-waiting: it checks the element is visible, enabled and still before clicking.
Tests run in parallel by default and are fast.
Built in: reports, screenshots, videos, trace viewer, API testing, network mocking.
Each test gets a fresh, isolated browser context (like a brand-new incognito window).

quiz.question: The button appears 2 seconds late. What does `click()` do?
quiz.why: Auto-wait is the superpower: click() waits until the element is ready (up to the timeout).

deep.text: Flaky tests: why they happen

A test is flaky when it sometimes passes and sometimes fails with no code change. The usual cause: the test is faster than the page. It clicks before the button is ready, or reads text before it appears. Playwright's auto-wait and retrying assertions fix most of this by design.
Isolation = reliable tests
Each Playwright test runs in its own fresh context. Test A logging in cannot affect test B. In Selenium you often had to remember to clear cookies or restart the driver.
Speed

deep.title: Run 100 tests in parallel on 4 workers
deep.code: npx playwright test --workers=4

deep.text: Because contexts are cheap (milliseconds) and workers are separate processes, suites that took an hour in Selenium often take minutes.
Playwright is not magic. Bad locators, shared test data and missing `await` still cause flaky tests. We'll learn how to avoid each one.

moreQuiz.why: A new context per test means no leaked cookies or state.

lessons.story: In Java you had the JDK, Maven and a `pom.xml`. Here, `Node` is the engine (like the JVM), `npm` is the package manager (like Maven), and `package.json` is the shopping list. `npx` is a handy tool that runs a program from your shopping list without installing it forever.

lessons.title: Variables and types
lessons.story: Variables are labelled boxes. A `const` box is glued shut: whatever you put in stays. A `let` box can be opened and changed later. You write the type after a colon, like a name tag: `age: number`.
lessons.codeCaption: TypeScript can often guess the type, so `const x = 5` is fine too.
points: Use `const` by default, `let` only when the value changes. Avoid `var`.
There is just one number type: `number` (no int, double, long).
Use `===` to compare (strict equals), not `==`.
Semicolons are optional but most people add them.

quiz.question: Which keyword lets you change the value later?
quiz.why: `let` boxes can be reassigned; `const` ones can't.

lessons.title: Functions and arrow functions
lessons.story: A function is a recipe card: give it ingredients, it gives you a dish. An arrow function is the same recipe written in a short, quick way using `=>`. You'll see arrows all over Playwright because tests themselves are written as arrow functions.
lessons.codeCaption: `(x) => ...` is exactly like Java's lambda `x -> ...`.
points: Java lambda `x -> x + 1` is TypeScript `(x) => x + 1`.
The return type goes after the parentheses: `): number`.
`console.log()` is your `System.out.println()`.

lessons.title: Arrays and objects
lessons.story: An array is a toy shelf where toys sit in a row. An object is a backpack with labelled pockets: `name`, `age`, `role`. Playwright hands you a backpack and says, "just take the pocket you need." That's called destructuring.
lessons.codeCaption: No need to create a class just to hold data. A plain object does it.
points: Objects are `{ key: value }`. Access with a dot: `user.name`.
Arrays are `[a, b, c]`. Loop with `for (const x of list)`.
`async ({ page }) => ...` is destructuring: pick `page` from the bigger object Playwright passes in.

quiz.question: In `async ({ page }) => {}`, the curly braces mean...
options: Pick `page` out of a bigger object
quiz.why: That's destructuring: Playwright passes an object full of helpers and you pick the ones you want.

lessons.title: async and await (the big one)
lessons.story: You order a pizza. The shop says "it's coming" (that's a `Promise`). If you start eating before it arrives, you eat air. `await` means: wait here until the pizza arrives, then continue. Every Playwright action is a pizza order, so every action needs `await`.
lessons.codeCaption: `await` only works inside a function marked `async`.
points: Browser actions take time, so they return a `Promise` (a "will finish later" ticket).
`await` pauses your test until the ticket is done.
Missing `await` is the number one beginner bug. Turn on the ESLint rule `no-floating-promises` to catch it.
`async` goes before the function; `await` goes before the action.

quiz.question: You forgot `await` before `click()`. What can happen?
options: The test runs the next step before the click finishes
quiz.why: Without await the code doesn't wait, so steps overlap and the test becomes flaky.

deep.text: What is a Promise?
A Promise is an object representing a result that isn't ready yet. It's either pending, fulfilled (success) or rejected (error). `await` unwraps it.

deep.text: Doing things at the same time
Sequential awaits run one after another. `Promise.all` runs things together and waits for all. You will use this for 'click and wait for the new tab' patterns.

lessons.title: Types, interfaces and generics
lessons.story: Types are name-tags that stop you putting a square toy in a round hole. TypeScript checks the tags before your tests run, so many silly mistakes (like typing `.clik()`) are caught while you type, not after a 10 minute run.
lessons.code:
type Status = 'pass' | 'fail';              // type alias with fixed choices
enum Env { Dev = 'dev', Prod = 'prod' }     // enum (strings are friendlier)

const names: Array<string> = [];             // same as string[]

function first<T>(list: T[]): T {            // generic, like Java's <T>
  return list[0];
}
const n = first(['a', 'b']);                 // n is a string
lessons.codeCaption: Generics use `<T>` just like Java.
points: A `type` alias gives a name to any type, even unions of exact words.
Avoid `any`. It switches the safety net off. Use `unknown` and check before use.
Red squiggles in VS Code are your friend. Read them.

quiz.question: What does `type Status = 'pass' | 'fail'` allow?
quiz.why: It's a union of literal values.
